title: US Proposes 30% H-1B Wage Hike, India GCCs Eye Windfall
excerpt: Entry-level H-1B salaries could jump to $98,000 as the Department of Labor overhauls prevailing wage rules for the first time in years
body:
The US Department of Labor has proposed raising minimum wages for H-1B visa holders by up to 30 percent, a move that could fundamentally reshape how Indian IT companies deploy talent across borders.

Under the proposed rule, published in the Federal Register and open for public comment until May 26, entry-level H-1B positions would carry a minimum salary of $97,746 — up from roughly $73,000 under current thresholds. Senior roles classified at Level IV would see floors rise to approximately $175,000. The wage bands would be recalibrated to the 35th and 90th percentiles of occupational wage data, replacing outdated benchmarks that critics argue have allowed employers to pay foreign workers below market rates for years.

**The GCC Equation:** For India's booming Global Capability Centers — the captive offshore units of multinationals like JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and Google — the math shifts decisively in their favor. If it costs $98,000 minimum to place a junior developer in Dallas, the case for hiring that same developer in Bengaluru at a third of the cost becomes irresistible. Industry body NASSCOM has long tracked the GCC boom: India now hosts over 1,700 GCCs employing more than 1.9 million people, and that number is projected to cross 2.5 million by 2030.

**What It Means for H-1B Workers:** The roughly 300,000 Indians who apply for H-1B visas annually face a paradox. Higher wages sound like good news — and for those who secure positions, it is. But employers, particularly mid-tier Indian IT services firms like Infosys, Wipro, and HCL, may sharply reduce the number of H-1B petitions they file if the cost of onshore deployment climbs 30 percent. Smaller staffing firms that have historically placed junior engineers at client sites could find the economics unworkable entirely.

The proposal arrives amid a broader tightening of the H-1B ecosystem. Filing fees have already jumped under recent USCIS reforms, and fraud investigations targeting so-called bench arrangements — where companies sponsor workers without confirmed placements — have intensified. Together, these pressures could produce the most significant contraction in Indian H-1B filings in over a decade.

**The Diaspora Ripple:** For the 4.4 million Indian-Americans, many of whom navigated the H-1B pipeline themselves, the wage hike crystallizes a tension at the heart of skilled immigration. Higher floors protect against exploitation, but they also narrow the gateway. Indian professionals already in the US on H-1B visas may see their renewal petitions become more expensive for employers to justify, adding pressure during an already uncertain green card backlog that stretches decades for India-born applicants.

**What to Watch:** The public comment period closes May 26. If finalized, the rule would take effect in late 2026, giving companies one budget cycle to adjust. Watch for lobbying from the US Chamber of Commerce and Indian IT industry bodies pushing for a phased implementation.
nri_angle: The proposed 30% H-1B wage hike directly impacts the 300,000 Indians who apply annually and the millions of Indian-Americans who navigated the same visa pipeline, potentially narrowing the gateway to skilled immigration while protecting against wage exploitation.
author: Diaspora Desk
